title: Dreaming of going to the Moon
text:
People have always looked up at the sky at night. They see the Moon, the stars and the planets moving slowly. And they wonder: what is up there? Could we go there?

In ancient times, many peoples believed the sky was the home of the gods. The Romans gave the planets the names of gods, which we still use: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn.

In the 2nd century, a Greek-speaking writer, Lucian of Samosata, wrote a very funny story called A True Story (which, of course, is completely made up!). His ship is carried up by a whirlwind all the way to the Moon. There he meets strange inhabitants and finds a war between the King of the Moon and the King of the Sun. It is one of the first stories ever written about a journey into space!

For centuries, other dreamers imagined crazy ways of reaching the Moon: a chariot pulled by wild geese, bottles of dew that rise as the Sun dries them, or even a giant cannon.

In China, a legend tells of an official named Wan Hu who tied 47 rockets to a chair to fly up into the sky. He is said to have vanished in a huge cloud of smoke! It is surely just a legend, but today a crater on the Moon bears his name.

For a long time, all this was only a dream. But these dreams would inspire scientists and engineers to find out how to do it for real...

title: Galileo points his telescope at the sky
text:
In 1609, an Italian scientist, Galileo, hears about a Dutch invention: a tube with lenses that makes faraway things look close. He builds a telescope himself, then an even more powerful one.

And he does something almost nobody had done before: he points it at the sky!

What he discovers is amazing:
- the Moon is not smooth and perfect, as people believed: it has mountains and [craters];
- the Milky Way is made of countless stars;
- four little moons are going around Jupiter! Today they are called the "Galilean moons";
- Venus changes shape, like the Moon.

At the time, most people think the Earth stands still at the centre of the Universe and the Sun goes around it. But Galileo's observations support another idea, put forward by the Polish astronomer Copernicus: it is the Earth that goes around the Sun! This is called [heliocentrism].

This idea upsets the Church of the time. In 1633, Galileo is put on trial and forced to say in public that he was wrong. He spends the rest of his life under house arrest. According to legend, he muttered: "And yet it moves!"

Galileo is one of the fathers of modern science: he showed that we must observe and measure to understand the world. And he opened people's eyes to how vast space is.

In 1989, NASA launched a probe to Jupiter named after him: Galileo.

title: Jules Verne: From the Earth to the Moon
refs: From the Earth to the Moon
text:
In 1865, a French writer, Jules Verne, publishes a novel that will make millions of readers dream: From the Earth to the Moon.

The story takes place in the United States. The members of a club of artillerymen, the Gun Club, are bored now that the war is over. Their president has a crazy idea: build a giant cannon to fire a shell all the way to the Moon! In the end, three men decide to travel inside the shell.

The cannon, called the Columbiad, is dug into the ground in Florida. In the sequel, Around the Moon (1869), the travellers circle the Moon, then fall back into the Pacific Ocean, where a ship picks them up.

Jules Verne had asked scientists lots of questions. And some of his ideas are surprisingly close to what really happened a century later with the Apollo 8 mission: three travellers, a launch from Florida, a trip around the Moon and a splashdown in the Pacific!

Of course, in real life a cannon wouldn't work: the push would crush the passengers. Another invention would be needed: the rocket.

Jules Verne's books inspired many space pioneers. The Russian Tsiolkovsky, the American Goddard and the German Oberth all said they wanted to build rockets after reading Jules Verne as children!

Today, a crater on the Moon and a European cargo ship that supplied the International Space Station are named after him. This kind of writing is called [science fiction]: imagining the future using science.

title: Tsiolkovsky works out the way to the stars
text:
Konstantin Tsiolkovsky was born in Russia in 1857. At the age of 10, he fell ill and became almost deaf. He could no longer go to school. So he taught himself, reading books in the library. He became a maths teacher in a small town.

Tsiolkovsky had a passion: space travel. He understood that no balloon, plane or cannon could ever get there. In space, there is no air to push against. The only way is the [rocket].

How does a rocket work? Imagine you are on a skateboard and you throw a heavy ball hard behind you: you roll forward! A rocket does the same thing: it throws very hot gases backwards at high speed, and that pushes it forwards. This is the principle of [action and reaction], discovered by Isaac Newton. It even works in empty space!

In 1903, Tsiolkovsky published a famous formula that works out how fast a rocket can go depending on how much fuel it carries. He also imagined rockets with several [stages] that drop their empty tanks along the way, space stations, spacesuits and even greenhouses in space!

He wrote a famous sentence: "The Earth is the cradle of humanity, but one cannot live in a cradle forever."

Tsiolkovsky never built a real rocket. He died in 1935. But his calculations were the starting point for everyone who built rockets after him. In Russia, he is called the "father of space travel".

title: Goddard launches the first liquid-fuel rocket
text:
Robert Goddard was an American physics teacher. When he was 17, while climbing a cherry tree, he dreamed of a machine that could fly up to Mars. He wrote the date in his diary and celebrated it for the rest of his life!

Rockets had existed for a long time: the Chinese invented gunpowder rockets almost a thousand years ago, for fireworks and for war. But they weren't powerful enough to reach space.

Goddard had an idea: use a liquid fuel, gasoline, burned with liquid oxygen, which is very cold. It is much more powerful, and the engine can be controlled.

On 16 March 1926, in a snowy field in Massachusetts on his aunt's farm, Goddard launched his first liquid-fuel rocket. It looked like a funny tangle of pipes. It rose 12 metres high and flew for two and a half seconds, before landing in a cabbage patch!

That may sound small, but it was as important as the Wright brothers' first aeroplane flight. It is the ancestor of all today's big rockets.

At the time, many people made fun of Goddard. In 1920, a big newspaper, the New York Times, even wrote that he didn't understand physics, because a rocket could not move in a vacuum. Goddard carried on anyway, and his rockets climbed higher and higher.

In 1969, the day after Apollo 11 left for the Moon, the New York Times published an apology: it admitted that a rocket really can work in a vacuum!

A big NASA centre is named after Goddard today.

title: The V-2: a weapon that reached space
text:
During World War II, Nazi Germany was looking for new weapons. A team of engineers, led by a young man passionate about rockets, Wernher von Braun, built a huge rocket: the V-2.

It was 14 metres tall and flew much faster than the speed of sound. From September 1944, thousands of V-2s were fired at London, Antwerp and other cities. They killed thousands of people. There was no way to stop them.

There is also a terrible truth behind this rocket: it was built in underground factories by prisoners from concentration camps, forced to work in horrible conditions. More people died building V-2s than were killed by them.

In June 1944, a V-2 fired straight up for a test climbed more than 170 kilometres high. It was the first human-made object to reach space! The edge of space is often set at 100 kilometres: this is called the "Kármán line".

At the end of the war in 1945, the Americans and the Soviets rushed to grab the German rockets, plans and engineers. Von Braun surrendered to the Americans. He would later build the Saturn V rocket, which took people to the Moon.

The story of the V-2 shows that the same technology can be used to destroy or to explore. At first, big rockets were built to carry bombs: these are called [missiles]. Only later were they used to travel into space.

title: Sputnik, the first satellite
text:
After World War II, two superpowers faced each other: the United States and the Soviet Union (the USSR, which included Russia). They didn't fight each other directly, but they were rivals in everything: this was the [Cold War].

Space would become one of the places where they competed. This was the "Space Race".

In the USSR, a brilliant engineer worked in secret: Sergei Korolev. His name was so secret that he was only called "the Chief Designer". He built a very powerful rocket, the R-7.

On 4 October 1957, the R-7 lifted off from Kazakhstan. It carried a small, shiny metal ball 58 centimetres across, with four long antennas: Sputnik 1, which means "travelling companion" in Russian.

Sputnik was placed in [orbit] around the Earth. It went all the way round in 96 minutes, at 28,000 km/h! It was the first artificial [satellite] in history.

Sputnik did just one thing: it sent out a little radio signal, "beep... beep... beep...". All over the world, radio fans could hear it. And at night, people could see the rocket stage that had launched it moving across the sky.

In the United States, it was a shock! Americans thought they were the most advanced. What if the Soviets could send bombs over their heads?

Sputnik's batteries ran out after 21 days. In January 1958, it fell back into the atmosphere and burned up. But the space age had begun!

title: Laika, the space dog
text:
Just one month after Sputnik, the Soviets wanted to do something even more impressive. But there was a big question: could a living creature survive the launch, [weightlessness] and the trip into space?

Before sending people, they sent animals. The Soviets chose stray dogs picked up from the streets of Moscow: they were used to cold and hunger, and they were calm.

On 3 November 1957, Sputnik 2 lifted off with a little three-year-old dog on board: Laika. She was the first living creature to go around the Earth in orbit. Sensors measured her heartbeat and breathing: she had survived the launch.

But there is a sad part: in 1957, nobody knew yet how to bring a spacecraft back to Earth. Laika's journey was one-way. Much later, we learned that she died a few hours after launch, because her cabin had become too hot.

Laika's fate moved the whole world. Today there is a statue of her in Moscow, and the engineers who worked with her later said they regretted it.

In 1960, two other dogs, Belka and Strelka, went around the Earth and came back alive! One of them later had puppies; the Soviet leader gave one to the daughter of American President Kennedy.

The Americans sent monkeys and apes, like the chimpanzee Ham in 1961. Mice, flies and tortoises have also travelled into space.

Thanks to these animals, we learned that people could survive up there.

title: Explorer 1 and the birth of NASA
text:
After Sputnik, the Americans wanted to respond fast. In December 1957, they tried to launch their own satellite on a rocket called Vanguard, in front of TV cameras. Disaster: the rocket rose about a metre, then exploded! Newspapers made fun of it, calling it "Flopnik" or "Kaputnik".

The US Army then turned to Wernher von Braun's team. On 31 January 1958, their Juno rocket put the first American satellite into orbit: Explorer 1. It was a long tube, 2 metres long, filled with scientific instruments.

And Explorer 1 made a big discovery! A scientist, James Van Allen, had put a radiation counter on board. He found that the Earth is surrounded by zones full of electrically charged particles, trapped by Earth's magnetic field. They are called the "Van Allen belts". Our planet's magnetic field protects us like an invisible shield!

On 29 July 1958, President Eisenhower created a new agency for space: NASA (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration). Its job was to explore space peacefully, for science. It opened its doors on 1 October 1958.

That same year, the United States also started new programmes to teach more science and maths at school, because they were afraid of falling behind the Soviets.

Today, NASA is the best-known [space agency] in the world. Its most famous centres are in Houston, Texas, where missions are controlled, and at Cape Canaveral, Florida, where rockets are launched.

title: The Luna probes and the far side of the Moon
text:
After the Earth, the next target was the Moon. To explore it, scientists sent machines with nobody on board, controlled from far away: [space probes].

In 1959, the Soviet Union achieved three firsts with its Luna probes:
- in January, Luna 1 passed near the Moon and became the first human-made object to escape Earth's pull. It is still going around the Sun today!
- in September, Luna 2 crashed on purpose into the Moon. It was the first human-made object to touch another world. It carried medals with the emblem of the USSR.
- in October, Luna 3 went around the Moon and took pictures of its far side.

The far side? The Moon spins exactly as fast as it goes around the Earth. As a result, it always shows us the same face! Before 1959, no human had ever seen the other side.

Luna 3's photos were blurry, but they showed a surprise: the far side is very different. It has far fewer big dark patches, the "seas", which are actually huge plains of cooled lava.

How could photos be sent from space in 1959? Luna 3 developed its film on board, like a tiny darkroom, then scanned the pictures and sent them by radio, line by line!

The Soviets gave Russian names to the mountains and craters they discovered, like the "Sea of Moscow" and the crater "Tsiolkovsky".

The far side is often called the "dark side", but that's wrong: it gets just as much sunlight as the side we see!

title: Yuri Gagarin, the first person in space
text:
Yuri Gagarin was born in 1934 in a small Russian village, into a family of farm workers. During the war, his family suffered a great deal. Later he became a factory worker, then a fighter pilot. He was short (1.57 metres), which was perfect for fitting into a tiny space capsule!

In 1960, he was picked from thousands of pilots to be one of the first Soviet [cosmonauts]. That is what space travellers are called in Russia; in the United States, they are called [astronauts].

On the morning of 12 April 1961, Gagarin climbed into the Vostok 1 capsule, a ball about two and a half metres across. As it lifted off, he cheerfully called out: "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!").

Vostok 1 went once around the Earth in 108 minutes. Through the porthole, Gagarin saw the Earth, the clouds and the oceans. He said: "The Earth is blue. How wonderful!"

The spacecraft was controlled automatically from the ground: nobody knew whether a person could think normally in weightlessness. On the way back, Gagarin ejected from the capsule 7 kilometres up and landed by parachute in a field, in front of a farm woman and her granddaughter, who were very surprised to see a man in an orange suit dropping from the sky!

Gagarin became the most famous hero in the world. He travelled to dozens of countries, always smiling.

He died in 1968 in a training plane crash, aged 34. Today, 12 April is celebrated all over the world as "Yuri's Night", the International Day of Human Space Flight.

title: Kennedy: "We will go to the Moon!"
text:
In 1961, Americans felt they always came second: first satellite, first animal, first person in space... all Soviet!

On 5 May 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space. But his flight lasted only 15 minutes: he went up and came down, without going around the Earth.

The young President of the United States, John F. Kennedy, wanted a challenge so huge that both countries would be starting from scratch, giving the Americans time to catch up. He asked his advisers: what spectacular thing can we do? The answer: send people to the Moon.

On 25 May 1961, speaking to the US Congress, Kennedy announced that the United States should, "before this decade is out, land a man on the Moon and return him safely to the Earth".

It was a crazy bet! At that moment, Americans had spent just 15 minutes in space. Nobody knew how to get to the Moon, how to land there, or how to come back.

In 1962, in a stadium in Houston, Kennedy gave another famous speech: "We choose to go to the Moon, not because it is easy, but because it is hard!"

This was the start of the Apollo programme. It would cost enormous sums and employ about 400,000 people: engineers, factory workers, seamstresses sewing the spacesuits, mathematicians working out the paths of the spacecraft...

Kennedy was assassinated in 1963. He never saw astronauts walk on the Moon. But the challenge he set was met.

title: John Glenn and the human computers
text:
On 20 February 1962, John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, aboard the capsule Friendship 7. He went around the Earth three times in nearly 5 hours.

During the flight, he saw thousands of little glowing specks around his capsule, like fireflies! They were actually bits of ice breaking off the spacecraft.

There was also a very scary moment: a warning light suggested that the heat shield, which protects the capsule from the terrible heat of coming back into the [atmosphere], might be loose. Luckily, it was a false alarm, and Glenn came back safe and sound. Millions of Americans followed his flight on TV.

Behind this success were heroines who stayed unknown for a long time. At NASA, mathematicians did very complicated calculations by hand. They were called "computers". Among them were several Black women, like Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson. At the time, because of [segregation], they had to work in a separate office and weren't allowed to use the same bathrooms as their white colleagues.

Before his flight, John Glenn didn't fully trust the new electronic computers. He asked for Katherine Johnson to check the machine's numbers herself: "If she says they're good, then I'm ready to go!"

Their story was told in 2016 in a film, Hidden Figures.

John Glenn went back into space in 1998, aboard the Space Shuttle, at the age of 77! At the time, he was the oldest person ever to go into space.

title: Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space
text:
Valentina Tereshkova was born in 1937 in a Russian village. Her father died in the war when she was two. She left school early to work in a textile factory, but kept studying in the evenings.

She had a passion: parachuting. She made about 90 jumps! That is what changed her life. In 1962, the Soviets were looking for women to go into space, and parachutists were wanted, because at the time cosmonauts had to jump out of their capsule and land by parachute.

On 16 June 1963, aged 26, Valentina Tereshkova lifted off aboard Vostok 6. Her radio call sign was "Chaika", which means "seagull".

She stayed in space for almost three days and went around the Earth 48 times! On her own, she spent more time in space than all the American astronauts put together up to then. She took photos of the horizon that helped scientists study the atmosphere.

The trip wasn't easy: she had space sickness, and her suit was uncomfortable. But she held on and came back a heroine.

Then it took 19 years for another woman to go into space: the Soviet Svetlana Savitskaya, in 1982. The first American woman, Sally Ride, flew in 1983, and the first French woman, Claudie Haigneré, in 1996.

Even today, Valentina Tereshkova is the only woman to have flown alone in space. She said: "If women can be railway workers, why can't they fly in space?"

title: Alexei Leonov, the first spacewalker
text:
On 18 March 1965, the Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov did something incredible: he climbed out of his spacecraft, Voskhod 2, and floated in the emptiness of space! It was the first [spacewalk].

To get out, he went through an inflatable airlock, a kind of fabric tube. Then he floated 5 metres from the spacecraft, attached by a cable. For 12 minutes he floated above the Earth. He said: "The Earth is round and it floats in the void... The silence was extraordinary."

But getting back in nearly ended in disaster! In the vacuum, his spacesuit had puffed up like a balloon. His hands no longer fitted in the gloves, his feet no longer in the boots. He couldn't get back into the airlock! Leonov took a risky decision: he let some of the air out of his suit to shrink it. At last he made it back inside, soaked in sweat.

And that wasn't all: on the way home, the automatic control broke down. The cosmonauts had to land by hand and came down in a snowy forest in the Ural Mountains, far from the planned spot. They spent two nights in the cold, surrounded by wolves, before rescuers arrived!

Leonov was also a very good artist. He had taken coloured pencils into space and made the first drawing ever done up there: a sunrise over the Earth.

Three months later, the American Ed White made his own spacewalk.

Today, astronauts often go outside the International Space Station to repair or install equipment.

title: Astérix: France becomes a space power
text:
During the Space Race, another country wanted its place too: France!

In 1961, General de Gaulle created the CNES (National Centre for Space Studies), the French [space agency]. French engineers developed a rocket called Diamant ("Diamond").

The tests took place in the Sahara Desert, in Algeria, at Hammaguir.

On 26 November 1965, Diamant lifted off and put a small 42-kilo satellite into orbit. Its name? Astérix, like the little Gaul from the comics who resists the Romans!

With this launch, France became the third space power in the world, after the Soviet Union and the United States. It was the first country after the two giants to launch a satellite on its own rocket.

Astérix had no scientific instruments: its job was to prove the rocket worked. It is still in orbit today, silent, and should stay there for centuries.

After Algeria became independent, France had to find a new place to launch its rockets. It chose Kourou, in French Guiana, in South America. Why there? Because it is close to the [equator]. At the equator, the Earth spins fastest, and that speed gives rockets a little extra push, like a slingshot!

The Guiana Space Centre opened in 1968. European Ariane rockets still launch from there today.

France gave the push that would later lead to the creation of the European Space Agency.

title: The Apollo 1 tragedy
text:
Space exploration was not just a series of successes. It also had tragedies, and we must remember them.

In early 1967, NASA was preparing the first flight of the Apollo spacecraft, the one that would one day go to the Moon. Three astronauts were chosen: Gus Grissom, Ed White (the first American to walk in space) and Roger Chaffee.

On 27 January 1967, they did a rehearsal on the launch pad in Florida, shut inside the capsule. The rocket had no fuel: it was only a practice.

Suddenly, a spark flew from a damaged electrical wire. The cabin was filled with pure oxygen, and many materials inside burned easily. In a few seconds the fire spread. The capsule's hatch opened inwards and was very hard to open. The three astronauts died.

All of America was heartbroken. The Apollo programme was stopped for more than a year and a half. Engineers went over everything: they changed the materials and the wiring, and designed a hatch that opens outwards in a few seconds.

Thanks to these changes, the following Apollo spacecraft were much safer.

That same year, in April 1967, the Soviet Union also lost a cosmonaut, Vladimir Komarov, when Soyuz 1's parachute failed to open on the way back to Earth.

The astronauts knew their job was dangerous. Gus Grissom had said: "The conquest of space is worth the risk of life."

title: Saturn V, the giant rocket
text:
To get to the Moon, you need an enormous rocket. Wernher von Braun's team built the biggest rocket ever used at the time: the Saturn V.

A few numbers to give you an idea:
- it was 110 metres tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty or a 36-storey building!
- it weighed nearly 3,000 tonnes at lift-off, as much as 400 elephants. Most of that was fuel;
- the five huge engines of its first stage burned 13 tonnes of fuel every second!

Saturn V had three [stages] stacked on top of each other. When the first stage had emptied its tanks, after about two and a half minutes, it dropped off and fell into the ocean. The second stage fired, then the third. Each time, the rocket became lighter and went faster. Right at the top was the small Apollo spacecraft with the three astronauts.

At lift-off, the noise was so loud it shook the ground kilometres away. The windows of the press buildings rattled. It is one of the loudest sounds ever made by humans, apart from explosions.

The rockets were put together standing up inside a giant building at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, so tall that clouds sometimes form inside! Then they were carried to the launch pad on a huge tracked vehicle, very slowly.

The first Saturn V launch, without a crew, took place on 9 November 1967. Thirteen Saturn Vs were launched, and none lost its crew.

title: Apollo 8 and Earthrise
text:
In December 1968, NASA made a daring decision: to send people around the Moon for the first time.

On 21 December 1968, three astronauts, Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders, lifted off aboard Apollo 8. They were the first humans to leave Earth's orbit and travel so far: nearly 400,000 kilometres!

Three days later, they reached the Moon and went around it ten times. They were the first humans to see the far side of the Moon with their own eyes.

On 24 December, as they came out from behind the Moon, they saw something nobody had ever seen: the Earth rising above the Moon's horizon, a small blue and white ball in the blackness of space. Bill Anders cried out: "Oh my God, look at that picture over there!" and quickly took a colour photo.

This photo is called Earthrise. It became one of the most famous photos in history. It shows how beautiful, small and fragile our planet is, lost in the vastness of space. It inspired the movement to protect the [environment].

On Christmas Eve, the astronauts made a TV broadcast from lunar orbit, watched by a billion people around the world.

Bill Anders later said: "We came all this way to explore the Moon, and the most important thing is that we discovered the Earth."

On 27 December, they came back safely in the Pacific Ocean. Just like in Jules Verne's novel!

title: Apollo 11: the first steps on the Moon
text:
On 16 July 1969, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Florida. Aboard Apollo 11 were three astronauts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins.

Four days later, on 20 July, Armstrong and Aldrin climbed into the [lunar module], called the Eagle, and went down towards the Moon. Collins stayed alone in orbit in the spacecraft Columbia.

The descent was very tense! Alarms went off in the onboard computer. Then Armstrong saw that the planned spot was full of big boulders. He took manual control and looked for a flat place. There was hardly any fuel left: less than a minute's worth! At last, the Eagle touched down. Armstrong announced: "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."

A few hours later, Armstrong climbed down the ladder. As he set foot on the Moon, he said: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

About 600 million people watched live on television, in black and white. In France, it was nearly 4 o'clock in the morning! Many children were woken up by their parents to watch.

Aldrin joined him. They walked for two and a half hours, taking little hops because of the Moon's low [gravity]. They planted an American flag, set up scientific instruments and collected 21 kilos of Moon rocks.

They left a plaque: "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind."

On 24 July, they came back to Earth. Kennedy's challenge had been met!

title: Apollo 13: "Houston, we've had a problem"
text:
On 11 April 1970, Apollo 13 lifted off for the Moon with three astronauts: Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise. It was meant to be the third Moon landing.

Two days later, more than 300,000 kilometres from Earth, there was a loud bang. An oxygen tank had exploded! Swigert told Earth: "Houston, we've had a problem."

The situation was very serious. The main spacecraft was losing its oxygen, water and electricity. There was no question of going to the Moon any more: they had to survive and get home.

The astronauts took shelter in the lunar module, built for two people for two days. The three of them had to last in it for nearly four days! To save electricity, they switched almost everything off. The temperature dropped to about 3 °C. They were cold, thirsty and got almost no sleep.

Another danger appeared: the carbon dioxide they breathed out was building up and could poison them. The filters from the main spacecraft were square, the ones in the lunar module round. On Earth, engineers came up with a solution using only what was on board: cardboard, sticky tape, plastic bags and a sock! The astronauts followed the instructions over the radio... and it worked!

To get back, the spacecraft swung around the Moon and used its [gravity] like a slingshot to head back towards Earth.

On 17 April, millions of people held their breath. After a few minutes of radio silence, the parachutes opened above the Pacific. The three astronauts were saved!

Apollo 13 was called "a successful failure": a lesson in keeping calm and working as a team.

title: Apollo 17 and the Blue Marble
text:
Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo missions landed on the Moon. In total, twelve astronauts, all American, walked on the Moon. Nobody has done it since!

The missions became longer and more scientific. From Apollo 15 onwards, the astronauts brought an electric car, the lunar rover, to go further. They set up instruments to measure moonquakes and brought back a total of 382 kilos of rocks.

Thanks to these rocks, scientists worked out how the Moon was born: about 4.5 billion years ago, a planet the size of Mars probably crashed into the young Earth. The debris thrown into space came together to form the Moon!

Apollo 17 was the last mission, in December 1972. For the first time, a scientist went along: the geologist Harrison Schmitt. He even found orange soil on the Moon! The astronauts stayed there for three days.

During the trip, the crew took a photo of the Earth fully lit by the Sun: you can see Africa, Antarctica and swirling clouds. It is called "The Blue Marble". It is one of the most widely shared images in history.

On 14 December 1972, before climbing back into the lunar module, Eugene Cernan said: "We leave as we came and, God willing, as we shall return, with peace and hope for all mankind." He also wrote his daughter's initials in the dust.

Since there is no wind or rain on the Moon, the astronauts' footprints are probably still there today!

title: The first space stations
text:
After the Moon, the Soviets and the Americans took on a new challenge: living in space for a long time. For that, you need homes orbiting the Earth: [space stations].

The Soviets were first. In April 1971, they launched Salyut 1. Three cosmonauts lived there for 23 days. Sadly, they died on the way back to Earth, because a valve opened and the air escaped from their capsule. Since then, astronauts always wear a spacesuit during launch and return.

In 1973, the Americans launched Skylab, built from a Saturn V rocket stage turned into a big house. During launch, a shield came loose and tore off a solar panel. Inside, it was over 50 °C! The first crew had to repair the station by putting out a kind of sunshade. They did it!

Three crews lived aboard Skylab, the last one for 84 days. They studied the Sun with a telescope, did experiments and learned how to live in weightlessness:
- they slept in sleeping bags attached to the wall;
- they showered inside a closed tube, where the water floated in droplets;
- they rode an exercise bike to keep their muscles and bones strong, because without [gravity], the body gets weaker.

Two spiders, Arabella and Anita, even went along to see whether they could spin webs in weightlessness. At first they struggled, then they managed it!

Skylab fell back to Earth in 1979. Pieces landed in Australia, luckily without hurting anyone.

title: Venera: photos from the hell of Venus
text:
Venus is the planet closest to Earth, and it is almost the same size. It is sometimes called Earth's "sister planet", or the "evening star", because it is the brightest thing in the sky after the Sun and the Moon.

For a long time, nobody knew what its surface looked like, because it is hidden under thick clouds. Some people even imagined jungles and swamps!

The Soviets decided to go and look. But Venus is a terrible place:
- it is about 460 °C, hot enough to melt lead! It is hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun;
- the air is so thick that it crushes everything: the pressure is 90 times stronger than on Earth, like being 900 metres under the ocean;
- the clouds are made of sulphuric acid.

Why is it so hot? Venus's atmosphere is almost all carbon dioxide, which traps the Sun's heat like a blanket. It is a giant [greenhouse effect]. By studying Venus, scientists better understand what could happen on Earth if we release too much carbon dioxide.

Several Venera probes were crushed before reaching the bottom. In 1970, Venera 7 became the first to land on another planet and send back data. In 1975, Venera 9 sent the first photos ever taken on the surface of another planet: ground covered with flat stones, under an orange sky.

The probes only survived a few dozen minutes before being cooked and crushed. In 1982, Venera 13 even sent colour photos!

title: Viking lands on Mars
text:
Mars, the red planet, has always fascinated people. In the 19th century, some astronomers thought they saw "canals" on its surface, and some imagined they had been dug by Martians! Many novels tell of aliens from Mars.

In the 1960s, the first American Mariner probes flew past Mars. No canals, no cities: a red desert full of craters. In 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet. It discovered giant volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the Solar System (about 22 kilometres!), and a huge canyon.

On 20 July 1976, exactly seven years after the first steps on the Moon, the American probe Viking 1 landed on Mars. Viking 2 joined it a few weeks later. They were the first probes to work for a long time on the surface of another planet.

The photos showed a desert landscape, with stones and dunes, and a pinkish-orange sky because of the dust. Mars is red because its soil contains lots of rust: iron oxide!

Viking had an important mission: to look for life. A robotic arm scooped up Martian soil and put it into mini-laboratories. The results were strange and hard to understand. Most scientists think no life was found, but people still argue about it today!

Viking 1 worked for more than six years. Since then, the exploration of Mars has never stopped.

title: Voyager and the Golden Record
text:
At the end of the 1970s, the Solar System's giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, were lined up in a way that happens only once every 176 years. A probe could hop from one to the next, using each planet's [gravity] like a slingshot to speed up!

In 1977, NASA launched two twin probes: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2.

Their journey was extraordinary:
- at Jupiter, they discovered erupting volcanoes on its moon Io: the first active volcanoes seen anywhere other than Earth;
- at Saturn, they photographed the rings in detail: they are made of thousands of thinner rings, made of chunks of ice;
- Voyager 2 is the only probe to have visited Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).

In 1990, Voyager 1 turned around to take one last photo of the Earth, from 6 billion kilometres away. It appears as a tiny pale blue dot in a ray of sunlight. The astronomer Carl Sagan wrote: "Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us."

On board each Voyager is a copper disc covered in gold, with a needle to play it. It is a message for any aliens who might find it! It contains pictures of Earth, sounds (wind, rain, a baby, whales), music from all over the world, and greetings in 55 languages.

Today, the Voyagers have left the area protected by the Sun and are travelling through [interstellar] space. Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object: more than 24 billion kilometres away! Its signals take almost a day to reach us.

title: Ariane, the European rocket
text:
In the 1970s, European countries realised that on their own, they could not compete in space with the United States and the Soviet Union. They decided to join forces.

In 1975, they created the European Space Agency, ESA. Today it brings together more than 20 countries.

Europe wanted its own rocket, so it would no longer depend on the Americans to launch its satellites. France proposed a project and paid for most of it: it would be called Ariane, after the princess in Greek mythology (Ariadne) who helped Theseus escape the labyrinth with a thread.

On 24 December 1979, the first Ariane lifted off from Kourou, in French Guiana. It was a success! A nice Christmas present for the engineers.

Ariane quickly became a great success. A company, Arianespace, was created to sell launches all over the world. In the 1990s, more than half of the world's commercial satellites were launched on Ariane rockets!

These satellites help us every day:
- [telecommunications] satellites carry television, phone calls and the Internet;
- weather satellites help forecast the weather and watch storms;
- others observe the Earth, its forests, oceans and climate.

Several generations followed: Ariane 4, then the powerful Ariane 5, which launched the James Webb Space Telescope in 2021. In 2024, the new Ariane 6 made its first flight.

Ariane shows that by working together, countries can achieve great things.

title: The Space Shuttle, a reusable spacecraft
text:
Until the 1970s, rockets were used only once. After launch, they fell into the ocean or burned up. That is very expensive! Imagine throwing away an aeroplane after every trip...

The Americans had an idea: build a spacecraft that takes off like a rocket but comes back and lands like a plane, so it can be used again. This was the [Space Shuttle].

The Shuttle had three parts:
- the orbiter, which looked like a big white plane with triangle-shaped wings, carrying the astronauts and a large cargo bay;
- a huge orange tank full of fuel;
- two white booster rockets, which parachuted into the ocean and were picked up.

On 12 April 1981, exactly 20 years after Gagarin, the Shuttle Columbia lifted off for the first time. Two days later, it landed in California like a glider. Success!

In total, five Shuttles flew: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour. Between 1981 and 2011, they flew 135 missions.

The Shuttle carried up to seven astronauts from many countries and jobs: scientists, doctors, teachers... Its big cargo bay could carry satellites, laboratories and even the Hubble telescope! It was also used to build the International Space Station.

But the Shuttle was very complicated and more expensive than planned. And it suffered two terrible accidents.

Today, the Shuttles are on display in museums in the United States. You can go and see them!

title: Jean-Loup Chrétien, the first Frenchman in space
text:
On 24 June 1982, Jean-Loup Chrétien, a French Air Force test pilot, lifted off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan aboard a Soviet Soyuz rocket. He became the first Frenchman and the first Western European to go into space!

At the time, it was the Cold War, and Europe was split in two. But France had been working with the Soviet Union on space projects since the 1960s. Chrétien had to learn Russian and train for two years near Moscow.

For a week, he lived aboard the Soviet space station Salyut 7 with four cosmonauts. He did scientific experiments, especially on the heart and on balance in weightlessness.

And being French, he brought... good food! Pâté, soup and pastries, prepared by chefs. They were the first "gourmet" meals in space, and the Soviet cosmonauts loved them!

In French, astronauts are sometimes called [spationautes]. Since Chrétien, about ten French people have gone into space, including:
- Patrick Baudry, aboard the American Space Shuttle in 1985;
- Claudie Haigneré, the first French woman in space in 1996, who later became a government minister.

In 1988, Jean-Loup Chrétien returned to space aboard the Mir station and became the first person who was neither American nor Soviet to do a spacewalk.

title: The Challenger and Columbia accidents
text:
On 28 January 1986, the Shuttle Challenger was getting ready to launch from Florida. On board were seven astronauts, including a teacher, Christa McAuliffe. She was going to give lessons from space, and millions of American children were watching on TV in their classrooms.

That morning it was very cold: there had been a frost in the night. 73 seconds after lift-off, the Shuttle broke apart in the sky. The seven astronauts died. It was a terrible shock, especially for the children who were watching.

The investigation found the cause: a rubber seal in one of the booster rockets had become stiff because of the cold. Burning gases escaped. Engineers had warned about the danger the day before, but nobody had listened to them.

On 1 February 2003, another tragedy happened. The Shuttle Columbia was coming back to Earth after a 16-day mission. During launch, a piece of insulating foam had broken off the tank and made a hole in the wing. On re-entry into the atmosphere, burning-hot air got into the wing. The Shuttle broke apart over Texas. The seven astronauts died, including the first Israeli astronaut, Ilan Ramon, and the Indian-born astronaut Kalpana Chawla.

These accidents were a reminder that travelling in space is still very dangerous. They taught an important lesson: always listen to people who report a problem, even when you are in a hurry.

Today, the names of the astronauts who died are written on a memorial in Florida, and many schools, craters and asteroids are named after them.

title: Mir, the record-breaking station
text:
In February 1986, the Soviet Union began putting together a new space station: Mir, which means both "peace" and "world" in Russian.

Mir was the first station built in several pieces, called [modules], launched one after another and joined together in space, like a giant construction set. In total, seven modules were added over ten years.

Mir broke many records:
- the doctor and cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov stayed aboard for 437 days in a row, more than a year! It is still the record for the longest single stay in space. He wanted to prove that a trip to Mars, which would last months, was possible;
- Mir was lived in almost non-stop for ten years;
- more than 100 astronauts from 12 countries visited it, including several French ones.

Life aboard wasn't always easy. In 1991, while the cosmonaut Sergei Krikalev was in space, the Soviet Union ceased to exist! He came back almost ten months after leaving, to a country with a new name: Russia.

In 1997, Mir had big problems: a fire on board, then a cargo ship crashed into a module. Air leaked out, and the crew had to shut a hatch quickly. Everyone was fine!

After the end of the Cold War, the old rivals became partners. From 1995, the American Shuttle came to dock with Mir. American and Russian astronauts lived together on board. It was practice for an even bigger station.

In March 2001, Mir was deliberately steered into the atmosphere. Most of it burned up, and the pieces left fell into the Pacific Ocean.

title: The Hubble Space Telescope
A planet found around another star
text:
The Sun is a star. And every star you see in the night sky is a sun, usually very far away. For a long time, scientists wondered: do these other suns have planets too?

It was very hard to find out. A planet is tiny next to its star, and it doesn't shine: it's like trying to see a firefly next to a lighthouse, thousands of kilometres away.

In 1995, two Swiss astronomers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, were watching a star called 51 Pegasi, about 50 [light-years] away, from the Haute-Provence Observatory in France. They noticed that the star was wobbling very slightly, back and forth, every four days.

Why? Because a planet was going around it and pulling on it a little with its gravity, just as a child spinning around while holding a grown-up's hand makes the grown-up move!

It was the first planet found around a star like the Sun. Such planets are called [exoplanets]. This one, 51 Pegasi b, is a huge ball of gas like Jupiter, but so close to its star that it is over 1,000 °C there!

Since then, astronomers have discovered more than 6,000 exoplanets, thanks to space telescopes like Kepler and the European mission CoRoT. Some are rocky like the Earth, and a few might have liquid water.

In 2019, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Is there life on one of these planets? It is one of the biggest questions in science!

title: Sojourner, the first robot on Mars
text:
On 4 July 1997, America's national holiday, the Mars Pathfinder probe arrived at Mars. To land, it used an amazing method: it was wrapped in giant airbags, like inflated balloons! It hit the ground, bounced about fifteen times, sometimes as high as a building, then stopped. The airbags deflated, and the probe opened like a flower.

Inside was a small passenger: Sojourner. It was a six-wheeled robot the size of a microwave oven, weighing 10 kilos. It was the first robot vehicle, a [rover], to drive on another planet.

Its name comes from Sojourner Truth, a Black American woman who fought in the 19th century against slavery and for women's rights. It was chosen through a school competition, won by a 12-year-old girl!

Sojourner drove very slowly, about one centimetre per second. It couldn't be steered live with a joystick: radio signals take several minutes to travel from Earth to Mars. So it had to be a bit independent and avoid obstacles on its own.

It analysed rocks, which scientists gave funny names: Barnacle Bill, Yogi, Scooby-Doo... They found rounded pebbles that may have been rolled by water a very long time ago.

The robot's mission was meant to last a week. It lasted nearly three months!

At the time, the Internet was brand new. Millions of people went to see the pictures of Mars on NASA's website: a record.

title: The International Space Station
text:
After the Cold War, the old rivals decided to build the biggest home in space together: the International Space Station, the ISS.

Five space agencies take part: those of the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. In all, 15 countries.

On 20 November 1998, the first module, a Russian one, was launched. Then, piece by piece, the station was assembled in orbit, using more than 40 rocket and Shuttle flights. It took more than ten years to finish.

The ISS is gigantic: it is the size of a football pitch, counting its huge solar panels. It weighs more than 400 tonnes. It circles the Earth 400 kilometres up, at 28,000 km/h: it goes around the Earth in 90 minutes! So the astronauts see 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.

You can see it pass overhead with your own eyes in the evening: it looks like a very bright star moving fast, without blinking.

Since November 2000, there have always been people on board, without a break! More than 280 people from over 20 countries have visited it.

On board, astronauts do experiments on plants, the human body and materials. They must exercise for two hours a day. Water is recycled, even sweat and urine, to become drinking water again!

The ISS shows that countries that were once enemies can work together. It is expected to be taken out of orbit around 2030.

title: Yang Liwei, the first Chinese astronaut
text:
China invented gunpowder rockets almost a thousand years ago. But for a long time, it couldn't send people into space.

In the 1990s, China started a big space programme. It built its own rockets, called Long March, and a spacecraft called Shenzhou, which means "divine vessel".

On 15 October 2003, an air force pilot, Yang Liwei, lifted off aboard Shenzhou 5 from the Gobi Desert. He went around the Earth 14 times in 21 hours, then landed in Inner Mongolia.

China became the third country able to send people into space on its own, after the Soviet Union (Russia) and the United States. Chinese astronauts are called [taikonauts], from the Chinese word "taikong", which means "space".

Yang Liwei became a national hero. Stamps and statues show him.

Since then, China has made huge progress:
- in 2008, a taikonaut made China's first spacewalk;
- in 2012, Liu Yang became the first Chinese woman in space;
- in 2021, China began assembling its own space station, Tiangong, which means "heavenly palace". Taikonauts live there all the time;
- it also sends probes to the Moon and to Mars.

Today, China has become one of the world's biggest space powers, and it plans to send taikonauts to the Moon before 2030.

title: Spirit and Opportunity look for water on Mars
text:
In January 2004, two twin robots landed on Mars, on opposite sides of the planet: Spirit and Opportunity. Like Sojourner, they landed wrapped in airbags. But they were much bigger: about the size of a golf cart.

Their mission: look for traces of water in Mars's past. Because where there is water, life might have been able to appear.

The two rovers had solar panels, cameras, a little brush and a kind of drill to scrape rocks, and instruments to find out what the rocks were made of. They were real robot geologists!

Opportunity made an important discovery: tiny balls of rock that scientists nicknamed "blueberries", and rocks that can only form in water. So, a very long time ago, Mars had liquid water on its surface, maybe lakes or seas!

The two robots were supposed to work for 90 days. But Martian winds sometimes blew the dust off their solar panels, which gave them fresh energy. Spirit worked for more than six years, until it got stuck in sand.

Opportunity drove for almost 15 years and more than 45 kilometres: longer than a marathon! In 2018, a gigantic dust storm hid the Sun for months. Opportunity ran out of energy and fell silent.

Its last message, put into simple words by a journalist, touched the whole world: "My battery is low and it's getting dark."

title: Huygens lands on Titan
text:
Saturn, with its beautiful rings, is a giant planet made of gas. More than 140 moons go around it! The biggest is called Titan. It is bigger than the planet Mercury.

Titan is mysterious, because it is wrapped in a thick orange atmosphere that hides its surface.

In 1997, NASA, the European Space Agency and the Italian Space Agency launched a big mission together: Cassini-Huygens. The trip to Saturn took almost seven years!

The Cassini spacecraft went into orbit around Saturn in 2004. It carried a small European probe, Huygens, named after the Dutch astronomer who discovered Titan in 1655.

On 14 January 2005, Huygens floated down by parachute through Titan's atmosphere for two and a half hours, taking photos. It landed gently. It is the most distant landing ever made: more than a billion kilometres from Earth!

The pictures showed an amazing landscape: hills, riverbeds and rounded pebbles. But on Titan it is -180 °C! The pebbles are made of ice as hard as rock, and the rivers aren't filled with water but with liquid [methane], a gas we use for cooking on Earth. It rains methane there!

Cassini studied Saturn for 13 years. It discovered that the little moon Enceladus shoots out geysers of water: there is an ocean hidden under its ice!

In 2017, running out of fuel, Cassini dived into Saturn, so that it wouldn't crash on a moon and contaminate it with germs from Earth.

title: Curiosity, a laboratory on Mars
text:
Curiosity is a giant rover: it is the size of a small car and weighs nearly a tonne. Too heavy to land with airbags!

To put it on Mars, engineers invented an incredible method, which they called the "seven minutes of terror". The spacecraft entered the atmosphere at 20,000 km/h, protected by a shield. Then it opened a huge parachute. Next, a kind of flying crane with rockets slowed down even more and lowered Curiosity on cables, like a crane dropping off a parcel! Once the robot had touched down, the crane flew off and crashed further away.

On 6 August 2012, everything worked perfectly. In the control room, engineers jumped for joy.

Curiosity is powered by the heat from a [radioactive] material, which lets it work even at night and in winter. It has 17 cameras, a robotic arm, a drill and a real little laboratory.

It also has a laser called ChemCam, partly designed in France! It fires at rocks several metres away and studies the light from the spark to work out what they are made of.

Curiosity discovered that the crater where it landed used to be a lake. It found molecules containing carbon there, which are "building blocks" of life, even though they can also form without life.

On its first birthday on Mars, Curiosity made one of its instruments vibrate to play "Happy Birthday" to itself!

More than ten years later, Curiosity is still driving and climbing a mountain 5 kilometres high.

title: Rosetta and Philae land on a comet
text:
[Comets] are huge chunks of ice, dust and rock that travel around the Sun. When they get close to the Sun, the ice turns into gas and forms a long, bright tail. They are leftovers from the birth of the Solar System, 4.6 billion years ago: studying them is like opening a very old memory box!

In 2004, the European Space Agency launched the Rosetta probe towards a comet with a complicated name: Churyumov-Gerasimenko, nicknamed "67P".

The journey took ten years! Rosetta went around the Sun several times and flew past Earth and Mars to pick up speed. For almost three years, it was put to sleep to save energy. In 2014, it woke up and sent the message "Hello, world!"

In August 2014, Rosetta reached the comet. Surprise: it looked like a giant rubber duck, 4 kilometres long!

On 12 November 2014, Rosetta dropped a little robot, Philae. It was the first attempt ever to land on a comet. But Philae had a problem: its harpoons didn't fire. It bounced twice and ended up stuck in a shady corner, where its solar panels didn't get enough light. It had just enough time to do its main measurements over about 60 hours, before falling asleep.

Rosetta studied the comet for two years. It found molecules that are important for life. In 2016, it gently touched down on the comet to end its mission.

The names Rosetta and Philae come from the Rosetta Stone and the obelisk of Philae, which helped scholars decipher hieroglyphs.

title: New Horizons finds Pluto's heart
text:
Pluto was discovered in 1930 by a young American astronomer, Clyde Tombaugh. For 76 years, it was considered the ninth planet of the Solar System. Its name was suggested by an 11-year-old English girl, Venetia Burney, who loved mythology: Pluto is the god of the underworld, where it is dark and cold.

But then many other small icy worlds were discovered beyond Neptune. In 2006, astronomers decided that Pluto would be a [dwarf planet]. Lots of children were sad!

In 2006, NASA launched the New Horizons probe towards Pluto. It is one of the fastest probes ever launched: it passed the Moon's orbit in just nine hours! But Pluto is so far away that it took almost ten years to get there.

On 14 July 2015, New Horizons flew 12,500 kilometres from Pluto. For the first time, we saw its real face.

And what a surprise! Pluto isn't just a grey ball of ice:
- it has a big, bright glacier shaped like a heart, named Tombaugh Regio;
- it has mountains of water ice as high as the Alps;
- its plains of nitrogen ice slowly move;
- its sky is bluish, with layers of haze.

The photos took months to arrive, because the probe is so far away and sends data very slowly.

On board New Horizons is a small container with some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered Pluto. So he got to make the journey to it!

New Horizons is still travelling today towards the edges of the Solar System.

title: SpaceX: rockets that come back and land
text:
For 60 years, almost every rocket was thrown away after one flight. It's as if you threw a plane in the bin after each trip! That's why going to space was so expensive.

In the 21st century, new private companies joined the space adventure. One of them, the American company SpaceX, wanted to make rockets [reusable].

Its idea: bring back the rocket's first stage, the most expensive part, and have it land by itself, upright, by relighting its engines and unfolding legs, like in science-fiction films!

The first tries were spectacular failures: the stages tipped over, toppled and exploded as they landed.

On 21 December 2015, the first stage of a Falcon 9 rocket came back and landed gently on a pad in Florida, after sending satellites into space. It was a historic first! A month earlier, Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket had already landed again, but after a short hop into space, without reaching orbit. Later, stages even landed on floating platforms in the middle of the ocean.

Today, some stages have flown more than 25 times. Launches have become much cheaper and much more frequent.

Since 2020, SpaceX has also carried astronauts to the International Space Station in its Crew Dragon capsule. Other companies and countries are also developing reusable rockets.

This raises questions too: thousands of small satellites are being launched to bring the Internet everywhere, which crowds the sky and gets in the way of astronomers observing the stars.

title: Chang'e 4 on the far side of the Moon
text:
Remember the far side of the Moon, photographed for the first time in 1959? For 60 years, no spacecraft had landed gently there. Why? Because the Moon blocks radio waves: from the far side, you can't talk directly to the Earth!

China found a clever solution. In 2018, it first sent a relay satellite, Queqiao, which means "Magpie Bridge". It sits behind the Moon and acts as a "bridge" to pass messages between the Earth and the far side.

On 3 January 2019, the Chinese probe Chang'e 4 landed in a big crater on the far side. It was a first in history! It set down a small rover called Yutu-2, the "Jade Rabbit".

Why those names? In a Chinese legend, Chang'e is a goddess who lives on the Moon with a white rabbit. Chinese people see a rabbit in the Moon's dark patches, where others see a face!

Chang'e 4 also carried a small experiment: a box with cotton seeds, potato seeds and fly eggs. A cotton seed sprouted! It was the first plant ever to grow on the Moon... even though it survived only a few days, because of the cold of the lunar night.

The little Yutu-2 rover drove for several years, a record for a robot on the Moon.

In 2020, another Chinese mission, Chang'e 5, brought Moon rocks back to Earth, the first since 1976. In 2024, Chang'e 6 even brought back the first samples from the far side!

title: Perseverance and Ingenuity, a helicopter on Mars
text:
On 18 February 2021, a new American rover landed on Mars: Perseverance. Its name was chosen by a schoolboy, Alexander Mather, through a competition.

Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, which used to be a lake, with a river flowing into it. It is a good place to look for traces of ancient life, such as fossilised microbes.

Perseverance has two big new features:
- it has microphones! For the first time, we can hear the sounds of Mars: the wind, and the noise of the rover driving;
- it collects rock samples in small tubes, which it leaves on the ground. A future mission is meant to come and fetch them and bring them back to Earth, to study them in real laboratories.

Its SuperCam instrument, a laser that analyses rocks, was largely built in France.

But the star of the show is a tiny passenger fixed under the rover: Ingenuity, a helicopter weighing 1.8 kilos! Flying on Mars is very hard, because the air there is a hundred times thinner than on Earth. To take off, its blades had to spin very fast: about 2,400 turns a minute.

On 19 April 2021, Ingenuity took off, flew 3 metres high for 39 seconds and landed again. It was the first powered flight on another planet! Just like the Wright brothers' first plane, a small piece of whose fabric was attached to the helicopter.

It was meant to fly five times. It flew 72 times, until 2024, when one of its blades broke!

title: The James Webb telescope sees the first galaxies
text:
On 25 December 2021, Christmas Day, a European Ariane 5 rocket lifted off from Kourou, in French Guiana. It carried the biggest and most powerful telescope ever sent into space: the James Webb Space Telescope.

Its main mirror is 6.5 metres wide, much bigger than Hubble's. It is made of 18 hexagon-shaped mirrors coated with a thin layer of gold! It is so big it had to be folded like origami to fit in the rocket. It then unfolded itself in space, following hundreds of steps. A single mistake, and everything would have been lost!

James Webb looks in the [infrared], a light our eyes can't see, which is linked to heat. To see very cold and very distant objects, it must be freezing cold itself: -230 °C. It is protected by a sunshield the size of a tennis court, made of five very thin layers.

It sits 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, four times further than the Moon.

In July 2022, the first images were released. They were dazzling! They show thousands of galaxies, clouds of gas where stars are born, and details never seen before.

James Webb sees light from galaxies that set off more than 13 billion years ago, not long after the Universe was born. Looking far into space means looking into the past!

It also studies the atmospheres of exoplanets, looking for water and perhaps, one day, signs of life.

Thanks to Ariane 5's very precise launch, it saved fuel and should be able to work for more than 20 years.

title: India lands near the Moon's south pole
text:
India started its space programme in the 1960s with very little money. It is said that early rockets were carried on bicycles and that parts of satellites travelled in bullock carts!

Little by little, the Indian space agency, ISRO, became very strong. In 2014, its Mangalyaan probe managed to go into orbit around Mars on its very first try, for less money than some Hollywood films cost to make!

In 2019, India tried to land a probe on the Moon, Chandrayaan-2. But at the last moment, the lander crashed. The engineers were very disappointed, but they didn't give up.

On 23 August 2023, the Chandrayaan-3 probe ("Moon craft" in Sanskrit) landed gently near the Moon's south pole. It was the first time any spacecraft had landed in that region! India became the fourth country to make a soft landing on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China.

In India, there were huge celebrations. Millions of people watched the broadcast, in schools and in public squares.

Why is the Moon's south pole so interesting? Because some craters there are always in shadow, and there might be [water ice] hidden at the bottom. That water would be very precious for future astronauts: they could drink it, turn it into oxygen to breathe, and even make rocket fuel!

The little Indian rover, Pragyan, drove about a hundred metres and confirmed that there is sulphur in the Moon's soil.

The landing day, 23 August, has become India's "National Space Day".

title: SpaceX's Starship: the tower catches the giant rocket
text:
After Falcon 9, the company SpaceX took on an even crazier project: Starship, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built.

It is about 120 metres tall, taller than the Saturn V that carried astronauts to the Moon! It has two parts:
- at the bottom, a huge first stage called Super Heavy, with 33 engines;
- at the top, the Starship spacecraft, which can carry cargo and, later, passengers.

Its goal: to be fully [reusable]. This time, both parts are meant to come back and fly again, like a plane that is refuelled after every trip. Its fuel is liquid methane and liquid oxygen, which might one day be made on Mars for the journey home.

Starship is built and tested in Texas, at a base called Starbase. The engineers learn by trying: the first test flights, from 2023, often ended in explosions. After each failure, they fix things and try again.

On 13 October 2024 came a spectacular moment. After launching the spacecraft, the Super Heavy first stage flew back to its launch tower. Two huge metal arms, nicknamed the "chopsticks", closed and caught it in mid-air as it came down slowly on its engines! Nobody had ever done that before.

NASA has chosen a version of Starship to land the astronauts of the Artemis programme on the Moon. And SpaceX dreams of using it one day to take people to Mars.

Starship is still being tested. But it shows how much rockets have changed since Goddard's little rocket, which flew for two and a half seconds!

title: Artemis: back to the Moon
text:
Since 1972, nobody has walked on the Moon. But many countries are interested in the Moon again!

NASA has started a big programme to go back: Artemis. In Greek mythology, Artemis is the goddess of the Moon and the twin sister of Apollo.

This time, the goal isn't just to plant a flag and leave. It is to stay longer, build a base near the south pole, where there may be ice, and learn to live far from Earth to prepare, later on, for the journey to Mars.

The programme has important goals:
- send the first woman and the first person of colour to the Moon;
- build a small station, called Gateway, in orbit around the Moon;
- work with other countries. Europe builds an essential part of the Orion spacecraft: the service module, which supplies electricity, water, air and propulsion.

On 16 November 2022, the giant SLS rocket lifted off from Florida for the Artemis I mission, without a crew. The Orion spacecraft went around the Moon and came back safely. On board, dummies measured radiation, and a little Snoopy toy floated to show when weightlessness began!

Artemis II is the programme's first mission with astronauts: four people, including a woman and a Canadian, on a trip around the Moon. The following missions are meant to land on the Moon.

China also plans to send taikonauts to the Moon. A new race may have begun!

title: Tomorrow, people on Mars?
Space in our everyday lives
